https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: German green group branded a Russian ‘puppet’ over Nord Stream II gas pipeline
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.subtitle: The Climate and Environmental Protection Foundation faces accusations that Moscow is funding it to bypass American sanctions on a controversial energy project
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
A German environmental foundation that has been given more than £17m by Gazprom, the Russian energy giant, has been accused of being a “puppet” funded by Moscow to circumvent American sanctions on the final stretch of a controversial pipeline carrying Russian natural gas to Germany.
The Climate and Environmental Protection Foundation was set up this month in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the largely rural state in northeast Germany where the 764-mile Nord Stream II pipeline comes ashore.
It is the creation of Manuela Schwesig, the state’s Social Democratic premier, who is an ally of Gerhard Schröder, Germany’s former chancellor and chairman of Nord Stream II.
Schröder has been attacked by political opponents for his close relationship with Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, with whom he reached the Nord Stream deal in 2005 shortly before leaving office.
The new foundation espouses a variety of green causes but also has a commercial wing that is authorised to buy parts and equipment for the pipeline, and is seen by Nord Stream’s opponents as a barely veiled attempt to circumvent sanctions.
Some €20m (£17.7m) of its budget comes from Gazprom, which leads the pipeline project – 100 times the €200,000 donated by the state government. The Russians are promising a further €40m in coming years. Nord Stream also has the right to name the head of the foundation’s commercial wing and other posts on its board.
“Frau Schwesig describes it as an environmental foundation. In fact, it’s a Gazprom Foundation,” Alexander Graf Lambsdorff, a senior member of the opposition Free Democratic Party and a leading critic of the project, told Deutschlandfunk radio.
“Ninety-nine per cent of the text of the articles of association is about climate and environmental protection, but 99 per cent of the money comes directly from Nord Stream II AG, which belongs to Gazprom.”
“It’s quite a curious foundation. It is a puppet construction,” said Sascha Müller-Kraenner, head of Environmental Action Germany, a green charity, which is challenging the legality of the organisation both in the German courts and with the European Commission.
The controversy has erupted as the government of Angela Merkel faces a battle with President Joe Biden over the Nord Stream II pipeline. When – or if – it is completed, it will carry together with the first Nord Stream, which has been operational for 10 years, a total of 110 billion cubic metres of gas a year.
Biden, like Donald Trump before him, opposes the project: he has called it a “bad deal for Europe” that will increase Russian economic and political leverage and cut out Ukraine, depriving it of the lucrative transfer fees it enjoys at present through a southern pipeline. Many of Germany’s fellow EU members, especially Poland and others in the east, share his misgivings.
Merkel, however, sees Nord Stream II as vital for Germany, which is in the process of phasing out nuclear power. Her stance is shared by Armin Laschet, who was elected head of Merkel’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party a fortnight ago and could become chancellor in September. Asked if he would reconsider his support, he said “no”, adding: “Germany decides.”
Backers of the pipeline see America’s opposition as motivated in large part by the desire of its own energy companies to sell liquefied shale gas to Europe – which is more expensive than the Russian gas.
The €9.5bn project has been shrouded in controversy since it was approved by Schröder weeks before he was beaten by Merkel in the 2005 general election. The former chancellor raised eyebrows by going on to become chairman of the boards of both Nord Stream and Rosneft, the Russian state-owned oil and gas company. Schröder has denied suggestions of conflict of interest.
Although work on the project is more than 90 per cent complete, it has been on hold since December 2019 when Allseas, a Swiss based offshore contractor that specialises in pipe laying, suspended its work after Trump signed off on sanctions, which the Biden administration is expected to continue.
Anger over the poisoning and arrest of Alexei Navalny, the Russian opposition leader, has further fuelled hostility. Bild, the German newspaper, accused Schröder of being “an errand boy for Putin” after he expressed doubts that Navalny was poisoned on the president’s orders.
The European parliament voted overwhelmingly 10 days ago for a stop to the project in protest at the Kremlin clampdown. Merkel’s government says it has “taken note” of the resolution, but Steffen Seibert, her spokesman, insisted last week: “There is no direct connection between the Navalny case and Nord Stream II.”
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the state premier has been open about the new foundation’s aim to help ensure completion of the pipeline.
“The new foundation will do many good things for environmental protection in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern over the years,” Schwesig told German media. “It will neither build nor operate the pipeline. But it can help build the pipeline if American sanctions make it necessary.”
Even if the pipeline is completed, further hurdles remain before the gas can start flowing. Russia will need a third party to certify the infrastructure but American legislation passed last December imposes sanctions on any company that does so or that insures it.
